newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin says tough year has made him a better man.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin says tough year has made him a better man.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin said on Thursday, the first anniversary of his re-election, that he had emerged a better man from the difficulties he faced over the last 12 months.
Yeltsin, now 66, defied the odds to fight off a communist challenge and win a four-year second term in an election run-off on July 3, 1996.

"For me it was not an easy year. It was a very difficult year. But this year changed me as a person and I am sure it changed me for the better," Interfax news agency quoted Yeltsin as telling reporters in the Kremlin.

He spent the first months of his new term fighting for his life because of heart problems but bounced back after surgery and then pneumonia to reaffirm his grip on power and give a new impetus to economic reforms.
Yeltsin said he had been congratulated by his family on Thursday morning but was working as usual. He began by having talks with President Haydar Aliyev of Azerbaijan in the Kremlin.

Yeltsin's allies, reflecting on the last year, gave him full marks for his political recovery after surgery. Some of his foes gave him grudging praise for some achievements, but others accused him of driving Russia down the road to ruin.
"It's total collapse," said Communist Party leader Gennady Zyuganov, whom Yeltsin defeated convincingly in the run-off.
Yeltsin is expected to touch on the achievements of the past year in a radio address on Friday, but has preferred until now to let Russia's economy do the talking for him.
Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin said on Wednesday that the economy was growing for the first time since the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991 and that economic reforms were working.
"To carry out these unpopular but necessary reforms, you need precisely the character of B. Yeltsin," Interfax quoted Sergei Belyayev, a pro-government parliamentarian, as saying.

Belyayev also praised Yeltsin's foreign policy, including an agreement improving ties with Slav neighbour Ukraine and a partnership agreement with NATO which reduced tensions over the Western defence alliance's expansion into eastern Europe.
Liberal Grigory Yavlinsky, who was eliminated in the first round of last year's election, hailed Russia's elevated role at a summit this year with the Group of Seven industrial nations.
But he is a critic of Yeltsin's economic policies and said his main achievement had been to get well.
"The president was ill for eight of the 12 months and, thank God, worked for four," he said.

Zyuganov meted out the most hostile criticism. "Not one of the president's many promises to the people has been carried out," Interfax quoted Zyuganov as saying and he described the year as one full of disappointments.
Newspapers on Thursday gave Yeltsin mixed reviews.

The popular Moskovsky Komsomolets asked "Boris Yeltsin: puppet or puppeteer?" The pro-communist Sovietskaya Rossiya, reviewing the six years since Yeltsin first became president, said "...the results get more and more regrettable each year."

Opinion polls suggest Yeltsin's popularity has sunk after rising sharply in the election campaign, when he gradually reduced Zyuganov's once huge lead by giving energetic performances across Russia and making lavish promises.
Yeltsin does not appear unduly worried by the loss in popularity -- the constitution bars him from seeking a third term.

First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais, on whom Yeltsin relied heavily when he was ill, hinted at Yeltsin's confidence when he said this week the president had granted him three weeks holiday this year. This, he said, was "astonishingly long".
